strings.b-00-meta.title: Laws of Motion
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can explain why Aristotle's idea that a force is needed to keep a body moving is wrong, and state Galileo's law of inertia.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can state and apply Newton's three laws of motion, including momentum, impulse and the conservation of momentum.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can analyse equilibrium, friction on level and inclined surfaces, and the circular motion of a car on level and banked roads.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can draw a free-body diagram and solve multi-body problems with the laws of motion.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: A body's resistance to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: Mass times velocity, p = m v; a vector pointing along the velocity.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: Force multiplied by the time it acts; it equals the change in momentum.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: The state of a particle when the net external force on it is zero.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: The part of a contact force that is perpendicular to the surfaces in contact.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: Self-adjusting friction that keeps a body at rest, up to the limit µ_s N.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: Friction that opposes actual sliding, equal to µ_k N.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: The name for whatever real force points towards the centre and provides the acceleration v²/R.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: A diagram of one chosen system showing only the forces acting on it from outside.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.9.definition: The speed √(R g tan θ) at which no friction is needed on a banked turn.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: Imagine a football lying still on the ground. To make it move, someone has to kick it. To send a stone upward, someone has to push it up. A breeze makes the branches of a tree swing, and a strong wind can even move heavy objects. In every one of these cases some outside agency supplies a force.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: Sometimes the agency touches the body, as your hand touches the ball or a flowing stream pushes a boat. This is not always necessary. A stone released from the top of a building speeds up downward because of the gravitational pull of the earth, and a bar magnet can attract an iron nail from a distance. So an external agency may act in contact or from a distance.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: Force is needed to stop motion too: you can stop a ball rolling down an inclined plane by pushing it against the direction of its motion.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.3: Now a sharper question. Suppose a body is already moving uniformly - a skater moving straight with constant speed on a horizontal ice slab. Is an external force required to keep it in uniform motion? This question looks simple, but it took ages to answer.
strings.b-02.paragraphs.0: Aristotle (384 B.C. - 322 B.C.) held that if a body is moving, something external is required to keep it moving. On this view an arrow shot from a bow keeps flying because the air behind it keeps pushing it. Put as a law: an external force is required to keep a body in motion.
strings.b-02.paragraphs.1: This feels natural from daily experience. A small child dragging a toy-car knows that the string must be pulled all the time; release it and the car comes to rest. Left to themselves, all bodies on the earth seem to stop.
strings.b-02.paragraphs.2: The flaw is friction. The moving toy-car stops because the floor exerts a force of friction on it, opposite to its motion. To keep the car going, the child must pull forward with an equal force, so that the net external force on the car is zero. If there were no friction, no force at all would be needed to keep the car moving uniformly.
strings.b-02.paragraphs.3: Opposing forces such as friction between solids, and viscous forces in fluids, are always present in the natural world. That is why we normally have to push things to keep them moving. To find the true law of nature, Galileo imagined a world with no friction at all.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: Galileo studied the motion of objects on inclined planes. An object moving down an inclined plane accelerates; an object moving up it retards. Motion on a horizontal plane is the in-between case. Galileo concluded that an object moving on a frictionless horizontal plane must neither accelerate nor retard: it moves with constant velocity.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: His second experiment used a double inclined plane. A ball released from rest on one plane rolls down and climbs the other. If the planes are smooth, the ball reaches nearly the same height as it started from - a little less, never more. With friction absent, the final height would equal the starting height.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.2: Make the second plane flatter and repeat: the ball still climbs to the same height, so it must travel farther. In the limiting case the second plane is horizontal and the ball travels an infinite distance - its motion never ceases.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.3: In practice the ball does stop after a finite distance, because friction can never be totally removed. Galileo's insight was that the state of rest and the state of uniform linear motion are equivalent: in both cases there is no net force on the body. The property a body has of resisting a change in its state of rest or uniform motion is called inertia. Inertia means 'resistance to change'.
strings.b-04.question: A child drags a toy-car by a string along a floor. The car moves in a straight line with constant speed. Which statement is correct?
strings.b-04.options.0: An external force is needed to keep the car moving, so the net force on it is not zero.
strings.b-04.options.1: The force by the child is balanced by the force of friction by the floor, so the net external force on the car is zero.
strings.b-04.options.2: The car has no inertia because it is moving.
strings.b-04.options.3: The car would speed up if the string were released.
strings.b-04.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by the first law the net external force must be zero. The child's pull and friction are equal and opposite. With no friction, no pull would be needed at all - which is exactly where Aristotle went wrong.
strings.b-05.question: In Galileo's double inclined plane experiment the planes are smooth. What happens as the slope of the second plane is made flatter and flatter?
strings.b-05.options.0: The ball climbs to a greater height than the height it started from.
strings.b-05.options.1: The ball reaches the same height but travels a longer distance, and with a horizontal second plane it would travel for ever.
strings.b-05.options.2: The ball stops on the second plane after a fixed distance, whatever the slope.
strings.b-05.options.3: The ball rolls back down the first plane.
strings.b-05.explanation: The ball always climbs back to nearly its starting height. A flatter plane means it needs more distance to reach that height, and on a horizontal plane the required distance is infinite - the idealised motion never ceases.
strings.b-06.caption: A book at rest on a table (left). The two forces on the book are its weight W, acting vertically downward, and the normal reaction R of the table, acting vertically upward. They are drawn equal in length because, with the book at rest, R must equal W. Directions only; the arrows show the two forces, not a measured scale.

strings.b-07.paragraphs.0: Newton built on Galileo's ideas and laid the foundation of mechanics in three laws of motion. Galileo's law of inertia became the first law: every body continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to act otherwise.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.1: Rest and uniform motion in a straight line both mean zero acceleration. So the first law can be said in one line: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero. Acceleration can be non-zero only if there is a net external force on the body.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.2: Two kinds of situation arise. Sometimes we know the net force is zero - for example a spaceship far from all other objects with all its rockets turned off; then its acceleration must be zero, and if it is moving it keeps a uniform velocity. More often we do not know all the forces, but we can see that the object is at rest or in uniform motion; the first law then tells us that the net external force on it must be zero.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.3: Take a book at rest on a table. Two forces act on it: its weight W downward and the normal force R of the table upward. The correct reasoning is not 'since W = R the forces cancel and the book stays at rest'. The correct reasoning is: the book is observed to be at rest, so by the first law the net external force on it must be zero, and therefore R must be equal and opposite to W. Gravity is everywhere and friction is common, so on the earth an object at rest or in uniform motion has forces on it that add up to zero - not no forces at all.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.4: You feel the first law in a bus. When the bus starts suddenly you are thrown backward: your feet move with the floor because of friction, while the rest of your body tends to stay where it was, because of inertia. When the bus stops suddenly your feet stop and the rest of your body keeps moving forward, so you are thrown forward.
strings.b-08.question: A drop of rain is falling vertically downward with a constant speed. What is the net external force on the drop?
strings.b-08.explanation: Constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration, so by the first law the net external force must be zero. The weight is balanced by the upward drag of the air. The forces are not individually zero - they cancel.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.0: The second law relates the net external force on a body to its acceleration, and it is stated in terms of momentum. The momentum of a body is defined as the product of its mass m and its velocity v, written p = m v. Momentum is a vector quantity; it points along the velocity.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.1: Why this product? A loaded truck needs a much greater force than a small car to reach the same speed in the same time, and a greater opposing force to stop in the same time at the same speed. A heavy stone is harder to catch than a light one dropped from the same height. A bullet fired at high speed can pierce tissue, while the same bullet at moderate speed does little damage. Mass alone, or speed alone, is not enough - the product m v is the quantity that matters.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.2: If a fixed force acts for a certain interval of time on two bodies of different masses, initially at rest, the lighter body picks up the greater speed; but at the end of that time each body has acquired the same momentum. The same force for the same time causes the same change in momentum for different bodies.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.3: Direction matters too. A stone whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed has a momentum of fixed magnitude whose direction keeps changing, and a force is needed to produce that change. Your hand must pull harder if you whirl the stone faster or in a smaller circle. So the greater the rate of change of the momentum vector, the greater the force.
strings.b-10.title: From momentum to F = m a
strings.b-10.steps.0.title: Step 1: momentum
strings.b-10.steps.0.detail: For a body of mass m moving with velocity v, the momentum is p = m v.
strings.b-10.steps.1.title: Step 2: the law in words
strings.b-10.steps.1.detail: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts.
strings.b-10.steps.2.title: Step 3: write it in symbols
strings.b-10.steps.2.detail: If a force F acts for a time interval Δt and the velocity changes from v to v + Δv, the momentum changes by Δp = m Δv. The law gives F ∝ Δp/Δt, that is F = k Δp/Δt with k a constant of proportionality.
strings.b-10.steps.3.title: Step 4: take the limit
strings.b-10.steps.3.detail: Let Δt become very small. Then Δp/Δt becomes the derivative dp/dt, so F = k dp/dt.
strings.b-10.steps.4.title: Step 5: fixed mass
strings.b-10.steps.4.detail: For a body of fixed mass, dp/dt = d(m v)/dt = m dv/dt = m a. So F = k m a.
strings.b-10.steps.5.title: Step 6: choose k = 1
strings.b-10.steps.5.detail: The unit of force has not been defined yet, so we are free to choose k = 1. Then F = dp/dt = m a. In SI units the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s-2 is one newton, so 1 N = 1 kg m s-2.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.0: Four points about the second law. First, putting F = 0 gives a = 0, so the second law agrees with the first. Second, it is a vector law: it is three equations, one for each component (F_x = dp_x/dt = m a_x, and similarly for y and z). A force not parallel to the velocity changes only the component of velocity along the force; the component perpendicular to the force stays unchanged - which is why a projectile under vertical gravity keeps its horizontal velocity component.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.1: Third, the law applies to a single point particle, and in the same form to a rigid body or a system of particles; then F is the total external force on the system and a is the acceleration of the system as a whole, with internal forces left out. Fourth, the law is a local relation: the force at a point at an instant determines the acceleration at that point at that instant. A stone dropped out of an accelerating train has, the moment after release, no horizontal force and no horizontal acceleration - it carries no memory of the train's acceleration.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.2: Remember also what F means. In F = m a, F is the net force due to all material agencies external to the body, and a is the effect of that force. The product m a is not one more force to be added to the list.
strings.b-12.problem: An astronaut accidentally gets separated out of his small spaceship accelerating in interstellar space at a constant rate of 100 m s-2. What is the acceleration of the astronaut the instant after he is outside the spaceship? (Assume that there are no nearby stars to exert gravitational force on him.)
strings.b-12.steps.0.title: List the forces
strings.b-12.steps.0.detail: There are no nearby stars to pull him, and the small spaceship exerts negligible gravitational attraction on him.
strings.b-12.steps.1.title: Net force
strings.b-12.steps.1.detail: So the net external force on the astronaut, once he is out of the spaceship, is zero.
strings.b-12.steps.2.title: Apply the first law
strings.b-12.steps.2.detail: If the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero.
strings.b-12.answer: The acceleration of the astronaut is zero. He does not keep the spaceship's 100 m s-2 acceleration, because force is not 'carried' by a body from its earlier motion.
strings.b-13.problem: A bullet of mass 0.04 kg moving with a speed of 90 m s-1 enters a heavy wooden block and is stopped after a distance of 60 cm. What is the average resistive force exerted by the block on the bullet?
strings.b-13.steps.0.title: Find the retardation
strings.b-13.steps.0.detail: Assume the retardation a is constant. From the speed u = 90 m s-1 and the stopping distance s = 60 cm = 0.6 m, a = u²/(2s) = (90 × 90)/(2 × 0.6) m s-2 = 6750 m s-2.
strings.b-13.steps.1.title: Apply the second law
strings.b-13.steps.1.detail: The retarding force is F = m a = 0.04 kg × 6750 m s-2.
strings.b-13.answer: F = 270 N. The actual resistive force, and therefore the retardation, may not be uniform, so this answer only indicates the average resistive force.
strings.b-14.problem: The motion of a particle of mass m is described by y = u t + ½ g t². Find the force acting on the particle.
strings.b-14.steps.0.title: Velocity
strings.b-14.steps.0.detail: Differentiate the position with respect to time: v = dy/dt = u + g t.
strings.b-14.steps.1.title: Acceleration
strings.b-14.steps.2.title: Force
strings.b-14.steps.2.detail: Apply the second law: F = m a = m g.
strings.b-14.answer: F = m g. The equation describes a particle moving under the acceleration due to gravity, with y the position coordinate measured in the direction of g.
strings.b-15.paragraphs.0: Some forces act for a very short time but are large enough to change momentum a lot - a ball hitting a wall and bouncing back, for example. The force on the ball acts only while ball and wall are in contact, and the force and the contact time are hard to measure separately. Their product is not hard: it is the change in momentum.
strings.b-15.paragraphs.1: That product is called impulse: impulse = force × time duration = change in momentum. A large force acting for a short time to produce a finite change in momentum is called an impulsive force. In Newtonian mechanics an impulsive force is not a separate kind of force - it is simply large and short-lived.
strings.b-15.paragraphs.2: This explains a familiar skill. A seasoned cricketer draws his hands backward while catching, so the ball takes a longer time to stop. The same change of momentum spread over a longer time needs a smaller force, so his hands are not hurt. A novice who holds his hands fixed must stop the ball almost instantly, needs a much larger force, and gets hurt.
strings.b-16.problem: A batsman hits back a ball straight in the direction of the bowler without changing its initial speed of 12 m s-1. If the mass of the ball is 0.15 kg, determine the impulse imparted to the ball. (Assume linear motion of the ball.)
strings.b-16.steps.0.title: Choose a positive direction
strings.b-16.steps.0.detail: Take the direction from the bowler to the batsman as positive. Initial momentum = 0.15 × 12 = 1.8 kg m s-1.
strings.b-16.steps.1.title: Final momentum
strings.b-16.steps.1.detail: After the hit the ball moves back with the same speed, so its final momentum is −1.8 kg m s-1.
strings.b-16.steps.2.title: Change in momentum
strings.b-16.steps.2.detail: Change in momentum = 0.15 × 12 − (−0.15 × 12) = 3.6 N s, and impulse equals this change.
strings.b-16.answer: Impulse = 3.6 N s, directed from the batsman to the bowler. The force on the ball and the time of contact are hard to know here, but the impulse is easy to calculate.
strings.b-17.question: A constant retarding force of 50 N is applied to a body of mass 20 kg moving initially with a speed of 15 m s-1. How long does the body take to stop? Give the answer in seconds.
strings.b-17.explanation: The retardation is a = F/m = 50/20 = 2.5 m s-2. That means the body loses 2.5 m s-1 of speed every second, so its 15 m s-1 is used up in 15/2.5 = 6 s.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.0: The second law tells you what an external force does; the third law tells you where such a force comes from. In Newtonian mechanics the external force on a body always arises from some other body. Press a coiled spring and the spring pushes back on your hand. The earth pulls a stone down, and the stone pulls the earth up with an equal and opposite force, which we do not notice because the earth is so massive.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.1: So force never occurs singly: force is a mutual interaction between two bodies, and forces always occur in pairs. Newton stated it as: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. In symbols, the force on A by B equals minus the force on B by A: F_AB = −F_BA.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.2: Three warnings. The words action and reaction mean nothing more than 'force'. There is no cause-and-effect order in them - the two forces act at the same instant, and either may be called action. And the two forces act on different bodies, so if you are studying the motion of one body, only one of the pair is relevant; adding them and claiming the net force is zero is an error. Only when both bodies are treated as one system do the pair become internal forces and cancel.
strings.b-19.problem: Two identical billiard balls strike a rigid wall with the same speed but at different angles, and get reflected without any change in speed. In case (a) a ball strikes the wall normally and bounces straight back. In case (b) a ball strikes the wall with its velocity at 30° to the normal and is reflected at 30° to the normal on the other side. What is (i) the direction of the force on the wall due to each ball, and (ii) the ratio of the magnitudes of the impulses imparted to the balls by the wall?
strings.b-19.steps.0.title: Set up axes
strings.b-19.steps.0.detail: Let u be the speed of each ball before and after the collision and m its mass. Take x along the normal to the wall, away from the wall as negative, and y along the wall.
strings.b-19.steps.1.title: Case (a): normal hit
strings.b-19.steps.1.detail: Initial p_x = m u, p_y = 0; final p_x = −m u, p_y = 0. So the x-component of impulse is −2 m u and the y-component is 0.
strings.b-19.steps.2.title: Case (b): hit at 30° to the normal
strings.b-19.steps.2.detail: Initial p_x = m u cos 30°, p_y = −m u sin 30°; final p_x = −m u cos 30°, p_y = −m u sin 30°. Only p_x changes sign, so the x-component of impulse is −2 m u cos 30° and the y-component is 0.
strings.b-19.steps.3.title: Use the third law
strings.b-19.steps.3.detail: Impulse and force are in the same direction. In both cases the impulse on the ball is normal to the wall; by the third law the force on the wall due to the ball is normal to the wall, in both cases.
strings.b-19.answer: The force on the wall is normal to the wall in both cases. The ratio of the impulse magnitudes is 2 m u /(2 m u cos 30°) = 2/√3, about 1.2. The magnitude of the force cannot be found, because the small contact time is not given.
strings.b-20.question: A book rests on a table. Which of the following is an action-reaction pair in the sense of Newton's third law?
strings.b-20.options.0: The weight of the book and the normal force of the table on the book.
strings.b-20.options.1: The force of gravity on the book by the earth, and the force of gravity on the earth by the book.
strings.b-20.options.2: The normal force of the table on the book and the weight of the table.
strings.b-20.options.3: The weight of the book and the weight of the table.
strings.b-20.explanation: An action-reaction pair is the two mutual forces between the same two bodies - here the book and the earth. The weight of the book and the normal force on it are two forces on the same body; they happen to be equal and opposite because the book is at rest, but they are not a third-law pair.
strings.b-21.paragraphs.0: The second and third laws together give the law of conservation of momentum. Fire a bullet from a gun. The force on the bullet by the gun is F; by the third law the force on the gun by the bullet is −F; both act for the same time interval. So the change in momentum of the bullet is F times that interval, and that of the gun is the opposite. Both start from rest, so their final momenta are equal and opposite, and the total momentum of the (bullet + gun) system stays zero.
strings.b-21.paragraphs.1: In an isolated system - one with no external force - the mutual forces between pairs of particles change the momentum of individual particles, but for each pair the changes are equal and opposite and cancel. So the total momentum remains unchanged. The law of conservation of momentum states: the total momentum of an isolated system of interacting particles is conserved.
strings.b-21.paragraphs.2: Collisions are the standard example. Two bodies A and B with initial momenta p_A and p_B collide and separate with momenta p′_A and p′_B. By the second law, using a common time of contact, F_AB times that time = p′_A − p_A and F_BA times that time = p′_B − p_B. Since F_AB = −F_BA, we get p′_A + p′_B = p_A + p_B: the final total momentum equals the initial total momentum. This is true whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.
strings.b-22.problem: A shell of mass 0.020 kg is fired by a gun of mass 100 kg. If the muzzle speed of the shell is 80 m s-1, what is the recoil speed of the gun?
strings.b-22.steps.0.title: Before firing
strings.b-22.steps.0.detail: Shell and gun are both at rest, so the total momentum of the system is zero.
strings.b-22.steps.1.title: Conservation of momentum
strings.b-22.steps.1.detail: There is no external force along the barrel, so the total momentum stays zero: mass of shell × speed of shell + mass of gun × speed of gun = 0.
strings.b-22.steps.2.title: Solve
strings.b-22.answer: The gun recoils with a speed of 0.016 m s-1, in the direction opposite to the shell.
strings.b-23.question: Two billiard balls, each of mass 0.05 kg, move in opposite directions with speed 6 m s-1, collide and rebound with the same speed. What is the magnitude of the impulse imparted to each ball due to the other? Give the answer in N s.
strings.b-23.explanation: Take one ball's initial direction as positive. Its momentum changes from 0.05 × 6 = 0.3 kg m s-1 to −0.3 kg m s-1. The change is 0.6 kg m s-1, so the impulse is 0.6 N s, directed opposite to that ball's original motion.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.0: A particle is in equilibrium in mechanics when the net external force on it is zero. By the first law, that means the particle is either at rest or in uniform motion.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.1: Under two forces F1 and F2, equilibrium requires F1 = −F2: the two forces must be equal and opposite. Under three concurrent forces F1, F2 and F3, equilibrium requires F1 + F2 + F3 = 0. The resultant of any two of them, found by the parallelogram law, must be equal and opposite to the third; the three forces can be drawn as the sides of a triangle with the arrows taken in the same sense.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.2: The result generalises to any number of forces: they keep a particle in equilibrium if they can be represented by the sides of a closed n-sided polygon with arrows in the same sense. In components, each of the x, y and z sums must vanish separately.
strings.b-25.problem: A mass of 6 kg is suspended by a rope of length 2 m from the ceiling. A force of 50 N in the horizontal direction is applied at the mid-point P of the rope. What is the angle the rope makes with the vertical in equilibrium? (Take g = 10 m s-2.) Neglect the mass of the rope.
strings.b-25.steps.0.title: Look at the suspended weight
strings.b-25.steps.0.detail: The weight is in equilibrium under its own weight and the tension T2 in the lower part of the rope, so T2 = 6 × 10 = 60 N.
strings.b-25.steps.1.title: Look at point P
strings.b-25.steps.1.detail: Three forces act on P: the tension T1 along the upper part of the rope, the tension T2 = 60 N along the lower part (vertically down), and the horizontal force of 50 N.
strings.b-25.steps.2.title: Resolve at P
strings.b-25.steps.2.detail: The vertical components must cancel: T1 cos θ = T2 = 60 N. The horizontal components must cancel: T1 sin θ = 50 N.
strings.b-25.steps.3.title: Solve
strings.b-25.steps.3.detail: Divide the two equations: tan θ = 50/60 = 0.83, so θ is about 40°. Then T1 = √(60² + 50²) ≈ 78 N.
strings.b-25.answer: The rope makes an angle of about 40° with the vertical. The answer does not depend on the length of the rope (assumed massless) or on the point at which the horizontal force is applied.
strings.b-26.question: Three concurrent forces act on a particle that is in equilibrium. Which statement must be true?
strings.b-26.options.0: Each force is equal in magnitude to the sum of the other two.
strings.b-26.options.1: The vector sum of the three forces is zero, and they can be drawn as the sides of a triangle with the arrows taken in the same sense.
strings.b-26.options.2: The three forces must be mutually perpendicular.
strings.b-26.options.3: The particle must be at rest, not moving.
strings.b-26.explanation: Equilibrium of a particle means zero net external force, so F1 + F2 + F3 = 0, and each component sum vanishes separately. The particle may also be in uniform motion, not necessarily at rest.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.0: Several kinds of force appear again and again in mechanics. The gravitational force is pervasive: every object on the earth feels the earth's pull, and gravity also governs the motion of celestial bodies. It acts at a distance, without any medium in between.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.1: All the other common forces are contact forces, arising when an object touches another object, solid or fluid. When two bodies are in contact there are mutual contact forces satisfying the third law. The component of the contact force normal to the surfaces in contact is called the normal reaction; the component parallel to the surfaces is called friction.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.2: Contact forces also arise between a solid and a fluid: a solid immersed in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced, and viscous force and air resistance are contact forces too. Tension in a string and the force of a spring are further examples. A spring compressed or stretched by an amount x exerts a restoring force F = −k x, where k is the force constant; the minus sign says the force is opposite to the displacement from the unstretched state.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.3: For an inextensible string the force constant is very high and the restoring force is called tension. For a string of negligible mass the tension T may be taken as the same throughout the string. At the microscopic level all these contact forces come from electrical forces between the charged constituents of the bodies, but their detailed origin is complex, so in mechanics they are treated as separate kinds of force whose properties are found by experiment.
strings.b-28.paragraphs.0: Put a block on a horizontal table. Gravity mg is cancelled by the normal reaction N. Now apply a small horizontal force F. The block may not move at all - yet if F were the only horizontal force it would have to accelerate. So another horizontal force must oppose F, keeping the net force zero. That force, parallel to the surface, is friction.
strings.b-28.paragraphs.1: While the block stays at rest, the friction is static friction f_s. It does not exist by itself: it appears the moment an applied force appears, and it grows to stay equal and opposite to the applied force. Static friction opposes impending motion - motion that would take place if friction were absent.
strings.b-28.paragraphs.2: Static friction has a limit. Experiment shows that the limiting value (f_s)max is independent of the area of contact and varies with the normal force as (f_s)max = µ_s N, where µ_s is the coefficient of static friction, a constant depending only on the nature of the two surfaces. So f_s ≤ µ_s N. When the applied force exceeds (f_s)max the block begins to slide, and the friction drops to a smaller value: kinetic (sliding) friction f_k = µ_k N, again independent of the area of contact and nearly independent of velocity, with µ_k less than µ_s.
strings.b-28.paragraphs.3: While sliding, the acceleration of the block is (F − f_k)/m; at constant velocity F = f_k exactly; remove the applied force and the acceleration is − f_k/m until the block stops. Notice that friction opposes relative motion, not motion: a box lying in the floor of an accelerating train is accelerated forward by static friction, and stays at rest relative to the train.
strings.b-28.paragraphs.4: A ring or sphere rolling without slipping would in principle feel no friction at all, since its single point of contact has no relative motion with the plane. In practice some rolling friction occurs, and for the same weight it is much smaller than static or sliding friction, even by 2 or 3 orders of magnitude - which is why the wheel has been such a milestone. Lubricants, ball bearings and a thin cushion of air reduce friction, but friction is also essential: brakes use kinetic friction to stop machines and vehicles, and we can walk only because of friction.
strings.b-29.caption: A block at rest on an inclined plane whose surface makes an angle θ with the horizontal (marked by the dashed horizontal line and the arc). Three forces act on the block: the weight mg vertically downward, the normal reaction N perpendicular to the sloped surface, and static friction fs up the slope, opposing the impending motion down the slope. Directions only; the arrows are not to a measured scale.
strings.b-30.problem: A mass of 4 kg rests on a horizontal plane. The plane is gradually inclined until at an angle θ = 15° with the horizontal the mass just begins to slide. What is the coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface?
strings.b-30.steps.0.title: Forces on the block
strings.b-30.steps.0.detail: Its weight mg acting vertically downward, the normal force N of the plane, and the static frictional force f_s opposing the impending motion.
strings.b-30.steps.1.title: Resolve the weight
strings.b-30.steps.1.detail: Along the slope the weight component is mg sin θ; perpendicular to the slope it is mg cos θ. In equilibrium mg sin θ = f_s and mg cos θ = N.
strings.b-30.steps.2.title: At the point of sliding
strings.b-30.steps.2.detail: As θ increases, the self-adjusting f_s increases until at θ_max it reaches its maximum value µ_s N. Then mg sin θ_max = µ_s mg cos θ_max.
strings.b-30.steps.3.title: The friction law for an incline
strings.b-30.steps.3.detail: Dividing gives tan θ_max = µ_s, and θ_max depends only on µ_s, not on the mass of the block.
strings.b-30.steps.4.title: Insert the numbers
strings.b-30.answer: µ_s = 0.27. Slightly beyond 15°, the small net force down the slope makes the block begin to slide.
strings.b-31.problem: A box lies on the floor of a train. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is 0.15. Determine the maximum acceleration of the train for which the box will remain stationary. (Take g = 10 m s-2.)
strings.b-31.steps.0.title: Which force accelerates the box?
strings.b-31.steps.0.detail: If the box is stationary relative to the train, it accelerates along with the train, and the only horizontal force available to do this is static friction.
strings.b-31.steps.1.title: Second law for the box
strings.b-31.steps.1.detail: m a = f_s, and static friction cannot exceed µ_s N = µ_s m g.
strings.b-31.steps.2.title: Inequality
strings.b-31.steps.2.detail: So m a ≤ µ_s m g, that is a ≤ µ_s g.
strings.b-32.problem: A 3 kg block hangs from a string that passes over a smooth pulley and is tied to a 20 kg trolley standing on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the trolley and the surface is 0.04. Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string. (Take g = 10 m s-2. Neglect the mass of the string.)
strings.b-32.steps.0.title: One acceleration
strings.b-32.steps.0.detail: The string is inextensible and the pulley smooth, so the 3 kg block and the 20 kg trolley have the same magnitude of acceleration a.
strings.b-32.steps.1.title: Equation for the block
strings.b-32.steps.1.detail: The block weighs 30 N and moves down: 30 − T = 3a.
strings.b-32.steps.2.title: Equation for the trolley
strings.b-32.steps.3.title: Add and solve
strings.b-32.steps.3.detail: Adding the two equations: 30 − 8 = 23a, so a = 22/23 m s-2.
strings.b-32.steps.4.title: Tension
strings.b-33.question: You push a block lying on a rough horizontal table with a small horizontal force. The block does not move. What is the friction force on the block at that instant?
strings.b-33.options.0: It is equal to µ_s N, whatever the size of your push.
strings.b-33.options.1: It is equal and opposite to your push, and smaller than µ_s N.
strings.b-33.options.2: It is zero, because the block is not moving.
strings.b-33.options.3: It is equal to µ_k N.
strings.b-33.explanation: Static friction is self-adjusting: it grows to match the applied force, up to the limit µ_s N. Only when the block is just about to slide does f_s equal µ_s N. Kinetic friction acts only after sliding has begun.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.0: A body moving in a circle of radius R with uniform speed v has an acceleration v²/R directed towards the centre. By the second law, the force providing this acceleration is f_c = m v²/R, also directed towards the centre. This force is called the centripetal force.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.1: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is only a name for whichever real force happens to point towards the centre: for a stone whirled on a string it is the tension in the string, for a planet going round the sun it is the gravitational pull of the sun, and for a car turning on a horizontal road it is the friction between the tyres and the road.
strings.b-35.title: Maximum speed of a car on a level road
strings.b-35.steps.0.title: Step 1: the three forces
strings.b-35.steps.0.detail: Three forces act on the car: its weight mg, the normal reaction N, and friction f.
strings.b-35.steps.1.title: Step 2: no vertical acceleration
strings.b-35.steps.2.title: Step 3: who supplies the centripetal force?
strings.b-35.steps.2.detail: The centripetal force must act along the road, towards the centre of the turn. The only horizontal force available is friction, so f = m v²/R.
strings.b-35.steps.3.title: Step 4: friction has a limit
strings.b-35.steps.3.detail: Static friction satisfies f ≤ µ_s N = µ_s m g.
strings.b-35.steps.4.title: Step 5: combine
strings.b-35.steps.4.detail: m v²/R ≤ µ_s m g gives v² ≤ µ_s R g. The mass cancels, so the answer is independent of the mass of the car.
strings.b-36.title: Maximum safe speed on a level circular turn
strings.b-36.description: On a level (unbanked) road friction alone supplies the centripetal force, so the maximum safe speed is v_max = √(µ_s R g). The plot draws this curve of v_max against the turn radius R for the coefficient of static friction you choose, and prints the value at your chosen radius. Take g = 10 m s-2.
strings.b-36.controls.mus.label: Coefficient of static friction µ_s
strings.b-36.controls.radius.label: Turn radius R (m)
strings.b-37.paragraphs.0: On a banked road the outer edge of the turn is raised, so the road surface makes an angle θ with the horizontal. The normal reaction then has a horizontal component pointing towards the centre, and friction has less work to do.
strings.b-37.paragraphs.1: There is still no acceleration in the vertical direction, so the vertical forces must cancel: N cos θ = mg + f sin θ. The centripetal force is supplied by the horizontal components of N and f together: N sin θ + f cos θ = m v²/R.
strings.b-37.paragraphs.2: To find the maximum permissible speed, put friction at its limit, f = µ_s N, and solve these two equations together.
strings.b-38.title: Maximum and optimum speed on a banked road
strings.b-38.steps.0.title: Step 1: put f at its limit
strings.b-38.steps.0.detail: Set f = µ_s N in the two banked-road equations: N cos θ = mg + µ_s N sin θ, and N sin θ + µ_s N cos θ = m v²/R.
strings.b-38.steps.1.title: Step 2: find N
strings.b-38.steps.1.detail: From the first equation, N = mg/(cos θ − µ_s sin θ).
strings.b-38.steps.2.title: Step 3: substitute
strings.b-38.steps.2.detail: Putting this N into the second equation and simplifying gives v²_max = R g (tan θ + µ_s)/(1 − µ_s tan θ).
strings.b-38.steps.3.title: Step 4: compare with the level road
strings.b-38.steps.3.detail: The maximum possible speed of a car on a banked road is greater than that on a flat road.
strings.b-38.steps.4.title: Step 5: switch friction off
strings.b-38.steps.4.detail: With µ_s = 0 the result becomes v_o = √(R g tan θ). At this optimum speed friction is not needed at all, so driving at it causes little wear and tear of the tyres. For v < v_o friction acts up the slope, and a car can be parked only if tan θ ≤ µ_s.
strings.b-39.problem: A cyclist speeding at 18 km/h on a level road takes a sharp circular turn of radius 3 m without reducing the speed. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.1. Will the cyclist slip while taking the turn? (Take g = 9.8 m s-2.)
strings.b-39.steps.0.title: The condition for not slipping
strings.b-39.steps.0.detail: On an unbanked road friction alone supplies the centripetal force, so the cyclist does not slip only if v² ≤ µ_s R g.
strings.b-39.steps.1.title: Convert the speed
strings.b-39.steps.1.detail: 18 km/h = 5 m s-1, so v² = 25 m2 s-2.
strings.b-39.steps.2.title: Compute the limit
strings.b-39.steps.3.title: Compare
strings.b-39.steps.3.detail: 25 m2 s-2 is much greater than 2.94 m2 s-2, so the condition is not obeyed.
strings.b-39.answer: The cyclist will slip. The speed is too large, or the turn too sharp, for friction to supply the needed centripetal force.
strings.b-40.problem: A circular racetrack of radius 300 m is banked at an angle of 15°. If the coefficient of friction between the wheels of a race-car and the road is 0.2, what is (a) the optimum speed of the race-car to avoid wear and tear on its tyres, and (b) the maximum permissible speed to avoid slipping? (Take g = 9.8 m s-2.)
strings.b-40.steps.0.title: (a) Optimum speed
strings.b-40.steps.0.detail: At the optimum speed the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone provides the centripetal force and friction is not needed: v_o = √(R g tan θ).
strings.b-40.steps.1.title: Insert numbers
strings.b-40.steps.2.title: (b) Maximum speed
strings.b-40.steps.2.detail: Use v_max = √(R g (tan θ + µ_s)/(1 − µ_s tan θ)).
strings.b-40.steps.3.title: Insert numbers
strings.b-40.answer: (a) Optimum speed ≈ 28.1 m s-1. (b) Maximum permissible speed ≈ 38.1 m s-1.
strings.b-41.paragraphs.0: Most real problems involve several bodies pushing and pulling on one another, and every one of them also feels gravity. The working method is always the same: choose any part of the assembly as your system and apply the laws of motion to it, provided you include all forces on that part due to the remaining parts of the assembly.
strings.b-41.paragraphs.1: Step by step: (i) draw a diagram of the assembly, showing the links and supports; (ii) choose a convenient part of the assembly as the system; (iii) draw a separate diagram of that system showing all the forces on it by the rest of the assembly and by other agencies, but not the forces it exerts on the environment. A diagram of this type is called a free-body diagram - and it does not imply that the system has no net force.
strings.b-41.paragraphs.2: (iv) On the free-body diagram, write in the forces whose magnitudes and directions are given or are certain, such as the direction of a tension along its length; treat the rest as unknowns to be found from the laws of motion. (v) If you need a second system, repeat the procedure and use the third law: if the force on A due to B is F in A's diagram, the force on B due to A is −F in B's diagram.
strings.b-42.problem: A wooden block of mass 2 kg rests on a soft horizontal floor. When an iron cylinder of mass 25 kg is placed on top of the block, the floor yields steadily and the block and the cylinder together go down with an acceleration of 0.1 m s-2. What is the action of the block on the floor (a) before and (b) after the floor yields? Take g = 10 m s-2. Identify the action-reaction pairs in the problem.
strings.b-42.steps.0.title: (a) Before: free-body diagram of the block
strings.b-42.steps.0.detail: Two forces act on the block: gravity 2 × 10 = 20 N downward, and the normal force R of the floor upward. The block is at rest, so by the first law R = 20 N.
strings.b-42.steps.1.title: (a) Third law
strings.b-42.steps.1.detail: The action of the block on the floor is 20 N vertically downward.
strings.b-42.steps.2.title: (b) Choose the system block + cylinder
strings.b-42.steps.2.detail: Its mass is 27 kg, so its weight is 270 N. The free-body diagram shows the weight 270 N downward and the normal force R′ of the floor upward; the internal forces between block and cylinder are not shown.
strings.b-42.steps.3.title: (b) Second law
strings.b-42.steps.3.detail: The system accelerates downward at 0.1 m s-2, so 270 − R′ = 27 × 0.1 = 2.7 N, giving R′ = 267.3 N.
strings.b-42.steps.4.title: (b) Third law and the pairs
strings.b-42.steps.4.detail: The action of the system on the floor is 267.3 N vertically downward. The pairs are: the pull of the earth on the block (or system) and the pull of the block (or system) on the earth; the push of the block (or system) on the floor and the push of the floor on the block (or system); and, after the floor yields, the force of the cylinder on the block and the force of the block on the cylinder.
strings.b-42.answer: (a) 20 N vertically downward; (b) 267.3 N vertically downward. The weight and the normal force are not an action-reaction pair: they act on the same body, and after the floor yields they are not even equal (270 N and 267.3 N).
strings.b-43.question: A man of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is moving downwards with a uniform acceleration of 5 m s-2. What is the reading on the scale? (Take g = 10 m s-2.) Give the answer in newtons.
strings.b-43.explanation: The scale reads the normal force N it exerts on the man. Taking downward as positive, the net downward force is mg − N = m a, so N = m(g − a) = 70 × (10 − 5) = 350 N. If the lift fell freely under gravity, a would equal g and the reading would be zero.
strings.b-44.question: A stone tied to a string is whirled round in a horizontal circle. The speed is increased beyond the maximum the string can bear, and the string breaks suddenly. Which describes the path of the stone from that instant?
strings.b-44.options.0: It moves radially outwards, away from the centre.
strings.b-44.options.1: It flies off along the tangent to the circle at the instant the string breaks.
strings.b-44.options.2: It flies off at an angle to the tangent, the angle depending on the speed.
strings.b-44.options.3: It continues round the same circle with a smaller speed.
strings.b-44.explanation: The tension of the string was the force changing the direction of the stone's momentum. The moment the string breaks, no horizontal force acts (neglecting air resistance), so by the first law the stone continues with the velocity it had at that instant - which is along the tangent - in a straight line.
strings.b-45.question: Why can a horse not pull a cart and run in empty space?
strings.b-45.options.0: Because there is no air in empty space to push against.
strings.b-45.options.1: Because the horse pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the horse and cart forward; in empty space there is no ground to push against, so no external forward force can act on the system.
strings.b-45.options.2: Because the mass of the horse is too small compared with the cart.
strings.b-45.options.3: Because friction between the cart and the ground would be too large in empty space.
strings.b-45.explanation: The forward force on the horse-and-cart system must come from outside that system. On the ground it is the friction between the horse's hooves and the ground: the horse pushes the ground backward, the ground pushes it forward. Without ground there is no such external force, and the mutual forces inside the system cannot accelerate it.
strings.b-46.paragraphs.0: Some mechanics problems give you a graph of position against time instead of a list of forces. You can still find the force, and the impulse, because everything follows from what the graph's slope is doing.
strings.b-46.paragraphs.1: For a particle, the velocity is the rate of change of position with time, v = dy/dt (take y as the position coordinate). On a position-time graph, this is the slope of the graph. The acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt, that is, how fast the slope itself is changing.
strings.b-46.paragraphs.2: Read the graph in three steps. If a stretch of the graph is a straight line, the velocity is constant there, so the acceleration is zero and, by the second law, the force on the particle during that interval is zero. If the slope changes steadily, the velocity is changing, so there is an acceleration and a force F = m a. If the slope changes abruptly at one instant - a kink in the graph - the velocity changes by a definite amount in almost no time, so the momentum changes abruptly: that change in momentum is the impulse delivered at that instant.
strings.b-46.paragraphs.3: The mass comes in twice: to turn the acceleration into a force, F = m a, and to turn a change of velocity into an impulse, impulse = change in momentum = m times the change in velocity. The force at any instant is fixed by the situation at that instant; a particle carries no memory of its earlier motion.
strings.b-47.problem: A stone of mass 0.25 kg tied to the end of a string is whirled round in a circle of radius 1.5 m with a speed of 40 rev./min in a horizontal plane. What is the tension in the string? What is the maximum speed with which the stone can be whirled around if the string can withstand a maximum tension of 200 N?
strings.b-47.steps.0.title: Who supplies the centripetal force?
strings.b-47.steps.0.detail: The stone moves in a circle at uniform speed, so it needs a force m v^2/R directed towards the centre. The only force acting towards the centre here is the tension in the string, so the tension is the centripetal force: T = m v^2/R.
strings.b-47.steps.1.title: Convert the speed to m s-1
strings.b-47.steps.1.detail: In one revolution the stone travels the circumference 2 pi R = 2 pi times 1.5, about 9.42 m. At 40 revolutions per minute it makes 40/60 of a revolution each second, so v = 9.42 times 40/60, about 6.28 m s-1.
strings.b-47.steps.2.title: Tension in the string
strings.b-47.steps.2.detail: T = m v^2/R = 0.25 times (6.28)^2 / 1.5, which is about 6.6 N.
strings.b-47.steps.3.title: Maximum speed from the maximum tension
strings.b-47.steps.3.detail: The string can give at most 200 N, so m v^2/R = 200 gives v = square root of (200 times 1.5 / 0.25) = square root of 1200, about 34.6 m s-1.
strings.b-47.answer: The tension is about 6.6 N. The maximum speed with which the stone can be whirled is about 34.6 m s-1; beyond that the string must supply more than 200 N and it breaks.
strings.b-48.problem: A pebble of mass 0.05 kg is thrown vertically upwards. Ignoring air resistance, give the magnitude and direction of the net force on the pebble (a) during its upward motion, (b) during its downward motion, and (c) at the highest point where it is momentarily at rest. (Take g = 10 m s-2.)
strings.b-48.steps.0.title: What forces act?
strings.b-48.steps.0.detail: Air resistance is neglected, so the only force on the pebble at any instant is its weight, mg, directed vertically downward. The earth is still pulling it whether it goes up, comes down, or hangs still for an instant.
strings.b-48.steps.1.title: Compute the weight
strings.b-48.steps.2.title: The highest point
strings.b-48.steps.2.detail: At the highest point the velocity is momentarily zero, but that does not make the force zero. Force and acceleration are fixed by the situation at the location of the body at that instant, not by how fast it happens to be moving: the force is still its weight mg and the acceleration is still g, downward.
strings.b-48.answer: (a) 0.5 N downward, (b) 0.5 N downward, (c) 0.5 N downward. The answer is the same in all three cases: a body momentarily at rest can still have a non-zero force and a non-zero acceleration.
strings.b-49.paragraphs.0: Why is it easier to pull a lawn mower than to push it? The answer comes from the two things you already know: the normal reaction and friction.
strings.b-49.paragraphs.1: When two surfaces are in contact, the contact force has a component normal to the surfaces, the normal reaction N, and a component parallel to them, friction. The laws of friction say that sliding friction is f_k = mu_k N (and static friction can rise at most to mu_s N). So the friction you must fight is proportional to the normal reaction: make N smaller and friction becomes smaller too.
strings.b-49.paragraphs.2: Pull the mower by a handle that slants upward, and your pull has an upward component. That upward component partly supports the mower, so the floor has to push up less: the normal reaction N becomes smaller, and with it the friction the mower has to overcome. Push the same mower with a handle slanting downward, and your push has a downward component that presses the mower harder into the ground: N becomes larger, and the friction is larger too. Same mower, same ground - only the direction of your force at the handle has changed, and with it the normal reaction and the friction.
strings.b-50.question: A particle of mass 4 kg has a position-time graph that is a straight line from t = 0 to t = 4 s, and a straight line of a different slope after t = 4 s. What is the force on the particle during the interval from t = 0 to t = 4 s?
strings.b-50.options.0: Zero, because the graph is a straight line there, so the velocity is constant and the acceleration is zero.
strings.b-50.options.1: 4 N, because the mass of the particle is 4 kg.
strings.b-50.options.2: Non-zero, because the particle is moving.
strings.b-50.options.3: It cannot be found without knowing the force after t = 4 s.
strings.b-50.explanation: A straight position-time graph means the velocity is not changing, so the acceleration is zero and by the second law the net force is zero. The force at any instant depends only on that instant, not on what happens after t = 4 s. At t = 4 s the slope changes abruptly, so the velocity changes suddenly and an impulse equal to that change in momentum is delivered there.
strings.b-51.question: A stone of mass 0.25 kg tied to a string of length 1.5 m is whirled round in a horizontal circle. If the string can withstand a maximum tension of 200 N, what is the maximum speed with which the stone can be whirled? Give the answer in m s-1, to one decimal place.
strings.b-51.explanation: The tension is the centripetal force, so m v^2/R = T gives v = square root of (T R / m) = square root of (200 times 1.5 / 0.25) = square root of 1200, about 34.6 m s-1. Beyond this speed the required centripetal force would exceed 200 N and the string would break.
strings.b-52.question: A pebble of mass 0.05 kg is thrown vertically upwards and, at the highest point of its path, is momentarily at rest. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s-2, what is the magnitude of the net force on it at that instant, in newtons?
strings.b-52.explanation: The only force is the weight mg = 0.05 times 10 = 0.5 N, directed downward, and it is the same at the highest point as anywhere else. Being momentarily at rest makes the velocity zero, not the force: the acceleration there is g, downward.
strings.b-53.question: Why is it easier to pull a lawn mower than to push it?
strings.b-53.options.0: Because pulling always needs a smaller force than pushing, whatever the angle.
strings.b-53.options.1: Because a pull on an upward-slanting handle reduces the normal reaction, and friction is proportional to the normal reaction, so there is less friction to overcome; a downward-slanting push increases both.
strings.b-53.options.2: Because the mower has less inertia when it is pulled.
strings.b-53.options.3: Because friction acts only when a body is pushed.
strings.b-53.explanation: Friction is the component of the contact force parallel to the surfaces, and its magnitude is proportional to the normal reaction N. An upward-slanting pull partly supports the mower, lowering N and hence friction; a downward-slanting push presses the mower into the ground, raising N and hence friction.

lesson.title: Laws of Motion
objectives: After this lesson you can explain why Aristotle's idea that a force is needed to keep a body moving is wrong, and state Galileo's law of inertia.
After this lesson you can state and apply Newton's three laws of motion, including momentum, impulse and the conservation of momentum.
After this lesson you can analyse equilibrium, friction on level and inclined surfaces, and the circular motion of a car on level and banked roads.
After this lesson you can draw a free-body diagram and solve multi-body problems with the laws of motion.

sections.title: Why we think a force is needed
paragraphs: Imagine a football lying still on the ground. To make it move, someone has to kick it. To send a stone upward, someone has to push it up. A breeze makes the branches of a tree swing, and a strong wind can even move heavy objects. In every case an outside agency supplies a force.

Sometimes that agency touches the body, as your hand touches the ball or a flowing stream pushes a boat. That is not always necessary: a stone released from a building speeds up downward because of the gravitational pull of the earth, and a bar magnet can attract an iron nail from a distance. So an external agency may act in contact or from a distance.

Force is needed to stop motion too. You can stop a ball rolling down an inclined plane by pushing it against the direction of its motion. Now a sharper question: if a body is already moving uniformly, like a skater gliding straight with constant speed on a horizontal ice slab, is an external force required to keep it in uniform motion? This question looks simple, but it took ages to answer.

sections.title: Aristotle's fallacy
paragraphs: Aristotle (384 B.C. - 322 B.C.) held that if a body is moving, something external is required to keep it moving. On this view an arrow shot from a bow keeps flying because the air behind it keeps pushing it. As a law: an external force is required to keep a body in motion.

This feels natural from daily experience. A child dragging a toy-car knows the string must be pulled all the time; release it and the car stops. Left to themselves, bodies on the earth seem to come to rest.

The flaw is friction. The toy-car stops because the floor exerts a force of friction opposite to its motion. To keep it going the child pulls forward with an equal force, so the net external force on the car is zero. If there were no friction, no force at all would be needed to keep the car in uniform motion.

Opposing forces such as friction between solids, and viscous forces in fluids, are always present in the natural world. That is why we normally have to push things to keep them moving. To find the true law of nature, Galileo imagined a world with no friction at all.

sections.title: The law of inertia
paragraphs: Galileo studied motion on inclined planes. An object moving down an inclined plane speeds up; an object moving up it slows down. Motion on a horizontal plane is the in-between case. Galileo concluded that an object on a frictionless horizontal plane must neither speed up nor slow down: it moves with constant velocity.

His second experiment used a double inclined plane. A ball released from rest on one plane rolls down and climbs the other. If the planes are smooth the ball reaches nearly the same height as it started from - a little less, never more. With friction absent, the final height would equal the starting height.

Make the second plane flatter and repeat: the ball still climbs to the same height, so it must travel farther. In the limiting case the second plane is horizontal and the ball travels an infinite distance, so its motion never ceases. In practice the ball does stop after a finite distance because friction can never be totally removed.

Galileo's insight was that the state of rest and the state of uniform linear motion are equivalent: in both there is no net force on the body. The property a body has of resisting a change in its state of rest or uniform motion is called inertia. Inertia means 'resistance to change'.

sections.title: Newton's first law of motion
paragraphs: Newton built on Galileo's ideas and laid the foundation of mechanics in three laws of motion. Galileo's law of inertia became the first law: every body continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to act otherwise.

Rest and uniform motion in a straight line both mean zero acceleration. So the first law can be said in one line: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero. Acceleration can be non-zero only if there is a net external force on the body.

Sometimes we know the net force is zero, for example for a spaceship far from all objects with its rockets turned off; then its acceleration must be zero and, if it is moving, it keeps a uniform velocity. More often we do not know all the forces, but we can see that an object is at rest or in uniform motion; the first law then tells us the net external force on it must be zero.

Take a book at rest on a table. Its weight W acts downward and the normal force R of the table acts upward. The correct reasoning is not 'since W = R the forces cancel and the book stays at rest'. It is: the book is observed to be at rest, so the net external force on it must be zero, which implies R is equal and opposite to W. Gravity and friction are everywhere, so a body at rest or in uniform motion has forces on it that add up to zero - not no forces at all.

You feel the first law in a bus. When the bus starts suddenly you are thrown backward: your feet move with the floor because of friction, but the rest of your body tends to stay where it was. When the bus stops suddenly your feet stop and the rest of your body keeps moving forward, so you are thrown forward.

sections.title: Newton's second law of motion: momentum and impulse
paragraphs: The second law relates the net external force on a body to its acceleration. It is stated in terms of momentum: the momentum of a body is the product of its mass m and its velocity v, written p = m v. Momentum is a vector, pointing along the velocity.

Why this product? A loaded truck needs a much greater force than a small car to reach the same speed in the same time, and needs a greater opposing force to stop in the same time. A bullet fired at high speed can pierce tissue, while the same bullet at moderate speed does little damage. Mass alone or speed alone is not enough; the product m v is the quantity that matters.

If a fixed force acts for a certain time on two bodies of different masses, the lighter body picks up the greater speed, yet each body acquires the same momentum. The same force for the same time causes the same change in momentum for different bodies. The second law says: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts.

Direction matters too. A stone whirled in a circle at constant speed has momentum of fixed magnitude whose direction keeps changing, and a force is needed for that change; your hand must pull harder if you whirl it faster or in a smaller circle. So the greater the rate of change of the momentum vector, the greater the force.

Four notes on the law. It agrees with the first law, since F = 0 gives a = 0. It is a vector law, three equations in all: a force not parallel to the velocity changes only the component of velocity along the force, which is why a projectile under vertical gravity keeps its horizontal velocity component. It applies to a particle and, in the same form, to a body or system of particles, with F the total external force and internal forces left out. And it is a local relation: the force here and now determines the acceleration here and now, not the history of the motion.

When a large force acts for a very short time, the force and the time are hard to measure separately, but their product equals the change in momentum. That product is called impulse: impulse = force × time duration = change in momentum. Such a large, short-lived force is called an impulsive force - no different in kind from any other force, only large and brief. A cricketer draws his hands backward while catching so that the same change of momentum takes a longer time and needs a smaller force; a novice who stops the ball almost instantly needs a much greater force and gets hurt.

sections.title: Newton's third law of motion
paragraphs: The second law tells you what an external force does; the third law tells you where it comes from. In Newtonian mechanics the external force on a body always arises from some other body. Press a coiled spring and the spring pushes back on your hand. The earth pulls a stone down, and the stone pulls the earth up with an equal and opposite force, which we do not notice because the earth is so massive.

So force never occurs singly: it is a mutual interaction between two bodies, and forces always occur in pairs. Newton stated it as: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. In symbols, F_AB = −F_BA: the force on A by B equals minus the force on B by A.

Three warnings. The words action and reaction mean nothing more than 'force'. There is no cause-and-effect order - the two forces act at the same instant, and either may be called action. And the two forces act on different bodies, so when you study the motion of one body only one of the pair matters; adding them and claiming the net force is zero is an error. Only when both bodies are treated as one system do the pair become internal forces and cancel.

sections.title: Conservation of momentum
paragraphs: The second and third laws together give the law of conservation of momentum. Fire a bullet from a gun: the force on the bullet by the gun is F, the force on the gun by the bullet is −F, and both act for the same time. So the bullet gains momentum F times that time and the gun gains the opposite amount. Both start from rest, so their final momenta are equal and opposite and the total momentum of the (bullet + gun) system is unchanged.

In an isolated system - one with no external force - mutual forces between pairs of particles change individual momenta, but for each pair the changes are equal and opposite and cancel, so the total momentum stays the same. The law states: the total momentum of an isolated system of interacting particles is conserved.

Collisions are the standard example. For two bodies with initial momenta p_A and p_B that collide and separate with momenta p′_A and p′_B, the second law gives F_AB times the contact time = p′_A − p_A and F_BA times the contact time = p′_B − p_B. Since F_AB = −F_BA, we get p′_A + p′_B = p_A + p_B: the final total momentum equals the initial total momentum. This holds whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.

sections.title: Equilibrium of a particle
paragraphs: A particle is in equilibrium in mechanics when the net external force on it is zero. By the first law that means the particle is either at rest or in uniform motion.

Under two forces, equilibrium requires them to be equal and opposite. Under three concurrent forces F1, F2 and F3, it requires F1 + F2 + F3 = 0: the resultant of any two, found by the parallelogram law, must be equal and opposite to the third. The three forces can then be drawn as the sides of a triangle with the arrows taken in the same sense.

The result generalises: forces keep a particle in equilibrium if they can be represented by the sides of a closed n-sided polygon with arrows in the same sense. In components, each of the x, y and z sums must vanish separately.

sections.title: Common forces in mechanics: friction
paragraphs: The gravitational force is pervasive: every object on the earth feels the earth's pull, and gravity also governs celestial bodies. It acts at a distance. All the other common forces are contact forces, arising when an object touches another object, solid or fluid.

The component of the contact force normal to the surfaces in contact is called the normal reaction; the component parallel to the surfaces is called friction. A solid immersed in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced; viscous force and air resistance are contact forces too. A spring compressed or stretched by x exerts a restoring force F = −k x, where k is the force constant and the minus sign says the force is opposite to the displacement from the unstretched state. For an inextensible string this restoring force is called tension, and for a string of negligible mass the tension T may be taken as constant throughout.

Place a block on a table and push it gently. It may not move, so some horizontal force must oppose your push, keeping the net force zero. That force, parallel to the surface, is friction. While the block stays at rest it is static friction f_s, which appears the moment an applied force appears and grows to match it. Static friction opposes impending motion - motion that would take place if friction were absent.

Static friction has a limit. Experiment shows (f_s)max is independent of the area of contact and is given by (f_s)max = µ_s N, where µ_s is the coefficient of static friction, depending only on the two surfaces. So f_s ≤ µ_s N. Beyond that limit the block slides, and friction drops to kinetic (sliding) friction f_k = µ_k N, again independent of the area of contact and nearly independent of velocity, with µ_k less than µ_s. While sliding, the acceleration is (F − f_k)/m; at constant velocity F = f_k; remove the applied force and the acceleration is − f_k/m until the block stops.

Friction opposes relative motion, not motion: a box lying in the floor of an accelerating train is accelerated forward by static friction and stays at rest relative to the train. A ring or sphere rolling without slipping would in principle feel no friction, since its single point of contact has no relative motion with the plane; in practice rolling friction does occur, and for the same weight it is much smaller than static or sliding friction, even by 2 or 3 orders of magnitude. Lubricants, ball bearings and a thin cushion of air reduce friction, but friction is also essential: brakes use kinetic friction and we can walk only because of friction.

sections.title: Circular motion
paragraphs: A body moving in a circle of radius R with uniform speed v has an acceleration v²/R directed towards the centre. By the second law the force providing it is f_c = m v²/R, also towards the centre, and is called the centripetal force. It is not a new kind of force: for a stone whirled on a string it is the tension, for a planet it is the sun's gravity, for a car turning on a level road it is friction.

On a level road, N = mg and friction alone supplies the centripetal force, so m v²/R ≤ µ_s m g and v_max = √(µ_s R g), independent of the mass of the car. On a banked road the surface is tilted by an angle θ, and the normal reaction itself has a horizontal component. Then N cos θ = mg + f sin θ and N sin θ + f cos θ = m v²/R; putting friction at its limit gives v_max = √(R g (tan θ + µ_s)/(1 − µ_s tan θ)), greater than on a flat road.

Putting µ_s = 0 gives the optimum speed v_o = √(R g tan θ), at which no friction is needed at all and tyres wear little. For v < v_o friction acts up the slope, and a car can be parked only if tan θ ≤ µ_s.

sections.title: Solving problems in mechanics
paragraphs: Most real problems involve several bodies pushing and pulling on one another, and every one of them also feels gravity. Choose any part of the assembly as your system and apply the laws of motion to it, provided you include all forces on it due to the remaining parts and other agencies.

The steps are: draw the assembly showing links and supports; choose a convenient part as the system; draw a separate diagram of that system with all forces on it by the rest of the assembly and other agencies, but not the forces it exerts on the environment - this is a free-body diagram, and it does not mean the system has no net force.

Then write in the forces whose magnitudes and directions are given or certain, such as the direction of a tension along its length, and treat the rest as unknowns. If you need a second system, repeat the procedure and use the third law: if the force on A due to B is F in A's diagram, the force on B due to A is −F in B's diagram.

paragraphs: Imagine a football lying still on the ground. To make it move, someone has to kick it. To send a stone upward, someone has to push it up. A breeze makes the branches of a tree swing, and a strong wind can even move heavy objects. In every one of these cases some outside agency supplies a force.

Sometimes the agency touches the body, as your hand touches the ball or a flowing stream pushes a boat. This is not always necessary. A stone released from the top of a building speeds up downward because of the gravitational pull of the earth, and a bar magnet can attract an iron nail from a distance. So an external agency may act in contact or from a distance.
Force is needed to stop motion too: you can stop a ball rolling down an inclined plane by pushing it against the direction of its motion.

Now a sharper question. Suppose a body is already moving uniformly - a skater moving straight with constant speed on a horizontal ice slab. Is an external force required to keep it in uniform motion? This question looks simple, but it took ages to answer.

Aristotle (384 B.C. - 322 B.C.) held that if a body is moving, something external is required to keep it moving. On this view an arrow shot from a bow keeps flying because the air behind it keeps pushing it. Put as a law: an external force is required to keep a body in motion.

This feels natural from daily experience. A small child dragging a toy-car knows that the string must be pulled all the time; release it and the car comes to rest. Left to themselves, all bodies on the earth seem to stop.

The flaw is friction. The moving toy-car stops because the floor exerts a force of friction on it, opposite to its motion. To keep the car going, the child must pull forward with an equal force, so that the net external force on the car is zero. If there were no friction, no force at all would be needed to keep the car moving uniformly.

Opposing forces such as friction between solids, and viscous forces in fluids, are always present in the natural world. That is why we normally have to push things to keep them moving. To find the true law of nature, Galileo imagined a world with no friction at all.

Galileo studied the motion of objects on inclined planes. An object moving down an inclined plane accelerates; an object moving up it retards. Motion on a horizontal plane is the in-between case. Galileo concluded that an object moving on a frictionless horizontal plane must neither accelerate nor retard: it moves with constant velocity.

His second experiment used a double inclined plane. A ball released from rest on one plane rolls down and climbs the other. If the planes are smooth, the ball reaches nearly the same height as it started from - a little less, never more. With friction absent, the final height would equal the starting height.

Make the second plane flatter and repeat: the ball still climbs to the same height, so it must travel farther. In the limiting case the second plane is horizontal and the ball travels an infinite distance - its motion never ceases.

In practice the ball does stop after a finite distance, because friction can never be totally removed. Galileo's insight was that the state of rest and the state of uniform linear motion are equivalent: in both cases there is no net force on the body. The property a body has of resisting a change in its state of rest or uniform motion is called inertia. Inertia means 'resistance to change'.

spec.question: A child drags a toy-car by a string along a floor. The car moves in a straight line with constant speed. Which statement is correct?
options: An external force is needed to keep the car moving, so the net force on it is not zero.
The force by the child is balanced by the force of friction by the floor, so the net external force on the car is zero.
The car has no inertia because it is moving.
The car would speed up if the string were released.
spec.answer: The force by the child is balanced by the force of friction by the floor, so the net external force on the car is zero.
spec.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by the first law the net external force must be zero. The child's pull and friction are equal and opposite. With no friction, no pull would be needed at all - which is exactly where Aristotle went wrong.
spec.expected_understanding: Separate 'a force is needed in practice' from 'a net force is needed'; friction is the force that must be overcome.

spec.question: In Galileo's double inclined plane experiment the planes are smooth. What happens as the slope of the second plane is made flatter and flatter?
options: The ball climbs to a greater height than the height it started from.
The ball reaches the same height but travels a longer distance, and with a horizontal second plane it would travel for ever.
The ball stops on the second plane after a fixed distance, whatever the slope.
The ball rolls back down the first plane.
spec.answer: The ball reaches the same height but travels a longer distance, and with a horizontal second plane it would travel for ever.
spec.explanation: The ball always climbs back to nearly its starting height. A flatter plane means it needs more distance to reach that height, and on a horizontal plane the required distance is infinite - the idealised motion never ceases.
spec.expected_understanding: The law of inertia is an extrapolation of the inclined plane experiments to zero slope.
